title: Infinitive Complements, Prepositional Patterns and Perfect Forms
summary: Choose verb patterns with and without an object before a to-infinitive; use required prepositions before an object and infinitive; distinguish the scope of negation; and describe earlier events with perfect infinitives and perfect -ing complements.
learningObjectives: Distinguish verbs that take object + to-infinitive from verbs that take a to-infinitive without an object.
Use for, at, on and to correctly in verb + preposition + object + to-infinitive patterns.
Explain the difference between negating the complement and negating the main verb.
Use perfect infinitives and perfect gerunds to locate an event before a later judgement or report.

explanation.heading: An object is required with some to-infinitive patterns
explanation.body: When advising, persuading, allowing, encouraging, warning or reminding a particular person, an active clause commonly uses verb + object + to-infinitive. The object identifies who is expected or enabled to act. By contrast, decide, agree, hope, offer, refuse and volunteer commonly take a to-infinitive without an object between the verbs. These are lexical patterns, not a free choice based on how much detail the speaker wants.
explanation.example: The organiser reminded the guests to register, but the organiser refused to extend the deadline.

explanation.heading: For before a different infinitive subject
explanation.body: Certain verbs and expressions need for before a person or thing that is the subject of an infinitive clause: arrange for someone to do something, wait for someone to arrive, or campaign for a measure to be adopted. Without for, these constructions may be ungrammatical or express a different pattern. Contrast this with persuade someone to act, which takes the object directly.
explanation.example: We arranged for the technician to inspect the lift before the conference.

explanation.heading: Other preposition + object + infinitive constructions
explanation.body: The preposition depends on the verb: call on somebody to act, depend on somebody to deliver, appeal to somebody to reconsider, signal to somebody to wait, and shout at somebody to move. Call on is a request, whereas depend on expresses reliance. The preposition is part of the verb construction and cannot generally be omitted. Context may permit other meanings with other prepositions, so learn the complete phrase.
explanation.example: The volunteers appealed to the organisers to reconsider the allocation.

explanation.heading: Negating the action is not negating the decision
explanation.body: Place not before a to-infinitive or gerund to negate the embedded action: agreed not to publish; considered not attending. Negating the main verb means something different: did not agree to publish tells us there was no agreement, not necessarily an agreement to remain silent. Similar differences arise between did not consider attending and considered not attending. Keep not next to the action or attitude whose truth you want to deny.
explanation.example: They decided not to release the figures; this is stronger than saying they did not decide to release them.

explanation.heading: Perfect infinitives and perfect -ing forms refer back
explanation.body: To have + past participle places an event earlier than the present assessment or reporting: appears to have left; is believed to have resigned. Having + past participle can place an action earlier than the reaction expressed by admit, deny, remember, recall or regret. A plain -ing form is often equally acceptable with the latter verbs and may communicate the same earlier action; the perfect form makes the time relationship explicit.
explanation.example: The reviewer seems to have missed the note, and later admitted having overlooked it.

comparisons.title: Verb + object + infinitive versus verb + infinitive

left.label: Persuade somebody to act
left.example: The editor persuaded the author to shorten the introduction.
left.note: The author is the person persuaded to act.

right.label: Agree to act
right.example: The author agreed to shorten the introduction.
right.note: Agree is followed directly by a to-infinitive in this meaning.

left.label: Negative complement
left.example: The committee agreed not to publish the names.
left.note: There was an agreement to withhold them.

right.label: Negative main verb
right.example: The committee did not agree to publish the names.
right.note: No agreement to publish was reached; withholding was not necessarily agreed either.

examples.sentence: The coordinator encouraged the speakers to submit their slides early.
examples.note: Encourage takes an object before the to-infinitive.

examples.sentence: The speakers volunteered to answer questions after the session.
examples.note: Volunteer can take a to-infinitive without a person object.

examples.sentence: We are counting on the supplier to deliver the replacement by Friday.
examples.note: Count on introduces the person relied upon before to deliver.

examples.sentence: Mina considered not accepting the offer until the terms were clarified.
examples.note: Not negates accepting, not the act of considering.

examples.sentence: The agreement is thought to have expired before the inspection.
examples.note: The perfect infinitive places the expiry before the present report.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The instructor reminded to bring our ID cards.
commonMistakes.correct: The instructor reminded us to bring our ID cards.
commonMistakes.why: In an active reminder addressed to people, remind takes the people as objects before the infinitive.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We arranged the translator to join the discussion.
commonMistakes.correct: We arranged for the translator to join the discussion.
commonMistakes.why: Arrange requires for before the infinitive subject in this construction.

commonMistakes.incorrect: They depended the courier to reach the office before six.
commonMistakes.correct: They depended on the courier to reach the office before six.
commonMistakes.why: Depend on somebody to do something contains the preposition on.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The missing parcel appears to disappear yesterday.
commonMistakes.correct: The missing parcel appears to have disappeared yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: A completed event yesterday is earlier than the present judgement, so a perfect infinitive is needed.

studyTips: Sort verb cards by the full frame: warn somebody to, decide to, arrange for somebody to and rely on somebody to.
Rephrase a decision twice, placing not before the main verb and then before the infinitive; explain the difference in meaning.
For earlier events, practise appears to have + past participle alongside regrets having + past participle, and test whether a plain gerund also works.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses a natural active pattern when an adviser urges an applicant to check their documents?
choices: The adviser encouraged the applicant to check the documents.
The adviser encouraged to check the applicant the documents.
The adviser encouraged for the applicant check the documents.
exercises.feedback: Encourage takes a person as an object before the to-infinitive.

exercises.prompt: The researcher ___ the findings at the conference, despite being nervous. Choose the verb pattern without an object before the infinitive.
exercises.feedback: Volunteer in this sense takes to + infinitive directly; it does not require a second person as an object.

exercises.prompt: The organiser arranged ___ join the call from overseas.
exercises.feedback: Arrange for somebody to do something requires for before the person who performs the action.

exercises.prompt: Today, the archivist concludes that the label was removed last month. Which sentence clearly preserves that earlier timing?
choices: The label appears to have been removed last month.
The label appears to remove last month.
The label appears removing last month.
exercises.feedback: Appears to have been removed uses a perfect passive infinitive for a prior event.

exercises.prompt: The head of the project reminded everyone ___ (submit) their forms. Write the complete to-infinitive.
exercises.feedback: Remind somebody to do something takes to submit after the person.

exercises.prompt: We are relying ___ the coordinator to make the final arrangements. Supply the required preposition.
exercises.feedback: Rely on somebody to do something expresses dependence on that person.

exercises.prompt: The committee agreed ___ (not / reveal) the names. Write the negative to-infinitive.
exercises.feedback: Agreed not to reveal indicates a positive agreement to withhold the names.

exercises.prompt: The actor denied ___ (sign) the contract before the meeting. Use having + past participle.
exercises.feedback: Having signed is a perfect -ing form locating the alleged signing before the denial.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The agency arranged the inspectors to visit on Monday.
acceptedAnswers: The agency arranged for the inspectors to visit on Monday.
exercises.feedback: Arrange for + object + to-infinitive is the required structure here.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The guide advised to keep our tickets until the exit.
acceptedAnswers: The guide advised us to keep our tickets until the exit.
exercises.feedback: The active advice concerns us, so advised requires us before the to-infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The residents appealed the council to reconsider the closure.
acceptedAnswers: The residents appealed to the council to reconsider the closure.
exercises.feedback: Appeal to somebody to do something uses to before the addressee.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The missing key seems to vanish sometime earlier this morning.
acceptedAnswers: The missing key seems to have vanished sometime earlier this morning.
exercises.feedback: Seems to have vanished refers to an event completed before the current assessment.

speakingExercises.prompt: The supervisor / warn / the contractors / wear / gloves. Say a complete past-tense sentence with an object and a to-infinitive.
acceptedAnswers: The supervisor warned the contractors to wear gloves.
speakingExercises.feedback: Warn takes the people addressed before the to-infinitive.

speakingExercises.prompt: The volunteer / offer / translate / the notices. Use past tense and no object between the verbs.
acceptedAnswers: The volunteer offered to translate the notices.
speakingExercises.feedback: Offer to do something directly precedes the infinitive.

speakingExercises.prompt: Facts: We / arrange / the camera operator / arrive early. Use arranged for and a to-infinitive.
acceptedAnswers: We arranged for the camera operator to arrive early.
speakingExercises.feedback: Arrange for somebody to do something identifies the person expected to act.

speakingExercises.prompt: Use depend on. Facts: They / depend on / Maya / solve the problem. Say one past-tense sentence.
acceptedAnswers: They depended on Maya to solve the problem.
speakingExercises.feedback: Depend on connects the person relied upon to an infinitive describing the expected action.

speakingExercises.prompt: Express a firm decision against attending. Facts: I / decide / not / attend / the briefing. Say a full past-tense sentence.
acceptedAnswers: I decided not to attend the briefing.
speakingExercises.feedback: Not to attend negates the chosen action, not the existence of the decision.

speakingExercises.prompt: Report a denial of an earlier act. Facts: She / deny / leak / the draft. Use past tense and the perfect gerund having leaked.
acceptedAnswers: She denied having leaked the draft.
speakingExercises.feedback: Having leaked refers back to the alleged earlier action.

speakingExercises.prompt: State a present inference about an earlier event. Facts: The bus / seem / depart / already. Use seems to have and the correct participle.
acceptedAnswers: The bus seems to have departed already.
speakingExercises.feedback: To have departed places the departure before the present inference.

speakingExercises.prompt: Give two distinct sentences in this order, using full forms: (1) no agreement to cancel; (2) an agreement not to cancel. Subject: The partners. Use the past tense.
acceptedAnswers: The partners did not agree to cancel. The partners agreed not to cancel.
speakingExercises.feedback: Negating agree and negating the infinitive are not equivalent.

listeningExercises.audioText: The manager reminded the guides to wear their identification badges before entering the museum.
listeningExercises.prompt: What did the manager remind the guides to do?
listeningExercises.feedback: Reminded the guides to wear introduces the required action.

listeningExercises.audioText: Following a lengthy discussion, the organisers agreed not to change the date of the exhibition.
listeningExercises.prompt: What decision did the organisers reach?
choices: They failed to discuss the date.
They agreed to keep the original date.
They agreed to cancel the exhibition.
listeningExercises.feedback: Agreed not to change establishes a deliberate decision to retain the date.

listeningExercises.audioText: We arranged for the interpreter to join the afternoon meeting remotely.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the eight-word phrase beginning with “for” and ending with “meeting”.
acceptedAnswers: for the interpreter to join the afternoon meeting
listeningExercises.feedback: Arrange for introduces the participant who will join the meeting.

listeningExercises.audioText: The computer appears to have restarted before the security update was installed.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which event is presented as having happened earlier?
listeningExercises.feedback: Appears to have restarted presents a completed restart before the later update installation.

listeningExercises.audioText: The captain signalled to the passengers to remain seated until the vehicle stopped.
listeningExercises.prompt: How did the captain communicate the instruction?
listeningExercises.feedback: Signalled to somebody to do something identifies an instruction communicated through a signal.

listeningExercises.audioText: The witness admitted having copied the spreadsheet but denied sharing it with anyone else.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which action did the witness admit?
listeningExercises.feedback: Admitted having copied states the earlier action that was acknowledged.

listeningExercises.audioText: The board called on the supplier to provide more evidence about the fault.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the seven-word phrase beginning with “on” and ending with “evidence”.
acceptedAnswers: on the supplier to provide more evidence
listeningExercises.feedback: Call on somebody to do something reports a request for action.

listeningExercises.audioText: The director regretted having ignored the initial warning about the delay.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the eight-word phrase beginning with “having” and ending with “delay”.
acceptedAnswers: having ignored the initial warning about the delay
listeningExercises.feedback: Regretted having ignored uses a perfect gerund to describe the earlier action.
